name: A1 — Beginner
description: First steps in Mandarin: greetings, numbers, basic verbs and questions.

topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Say hello, goodbye, and how are you

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.
How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 吗 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 吗 = 你好吗? ("are you good?").

lessons.title: Hello & goodbye
lessons.description: The two phrases you can't live without

exercises.explanation: "再见" literally means "see you again."

exercises.prompt: Match the greeting to its meaning

exercises.explanation: 你好 (nǐ hǎo) is the everyday hello — both syllables third tone, but the first becomes second tone in speech.

exercises.prompt: You meet your friend's grandmother for the first time. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: 您 (nín) is the polite "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers to show respect.
见 (jiàn) means "see/meet" — pair it with a time word to schedule a goodbye.
Putting 老师 first is a respectful way to address a teacher before the greeting.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT a way to say goodbye?
exercises.explanation: 拜拜 (bài bài) is borrowed from English "bye-bye" and is very common in casual speech.
Borrowed from English — common in informal goodbyes, especially over the phone.

lessons.title: How are you?
lessons.description: Ask after someone and answer back

exercises.prompt: How do you say "How are you?"

exercises.answer: 我 很 好 谢谢
exercises.explanation: In Mandarin, adjectives don't take 是 — "I am good" is literally 我很好 (I very good).

exercises.prompt: Your friend asks 你好吗? You're feeling fine. What do you say?
"不错" (bú cuò) literally "not wrong" — it means ___
exercises.explanation: Common, slightly understated way to answer "how are you?" — like English "not bad."

exercises.prompt: Match the response with its tone

exercises.explanation: Listen for 我 (wǒ, third tone — dipping) vs 你 (nǐ) and 他 (tā).
呢 (ne) bounces a question back. After answering 我很好, add 你呢 to ask the same of the other person.

exercises.prompt: Build: "How are you? And you?" — answer the first question with "and you?"
exercises.answer: 我 很 好 你 呢

exercises.prompt: "马马虎虎" (mǎ mǎ hū hū) literally "horse horse tiger tiger" means ___
exercises.explanation: A fun idiom — when neither good nor bad, you're "horse-tiger."

lessons.title: Polite phrases
lessons.description: Thank you, sorry, and you're welcome

exercises.explanation: Literally "don't be polite" — the standard reply to 谢谢.

exercises.prompt: Someone says 对不起 to you. What's the natural reply?
exercises.explanation: 没关系 (méi guān xi) means "it doesn't matter / it's okay" — the standard answer to an apology.
Place 请 at the start of a request to be polite, e.g. 请坐 (please sit).

exercises.prompt: Which is more emphatic for "thank you very much"?
exercises.explanation: 非常 (fēi cháng) = extremely; 感谢 (gǎn xiè) is a more formal "thanks." Together: "thanks a lot."

exercises.answer: 对不起 请 等 一下

exercises.explanation: Literally: "knowing you makes me happy."

exercises.prompt: What does "你叫什么名字" mean?
exercises.explanation: Literally: "You called what name?" 名字 (míng zi) = name.

exercises.answer: 你 叫 什么 名字

exercises.explanation: 我叫 (wǒ jiào) — "I am called." Listen for the falling tone on 叫.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between "我叫小明" and "我是小明"?
options: Both mean "my name is Xiao Ming" — 叫 is more common in casual intros
我叫 means "I want" and 我是 means "I am"
我叫 is past tense, 我是 is present tense
exercises.answer: Both mean "my name is Xiao Ming" — 叫 is more common in casual intros
exercises.explanation: 我叫 literally "I'm called" — natural, friendly. 我是 literally "I am" — slightly more formal.

exercises.prompt: "贵姓" (guì xìng) literally "honored surname" — used to ask ___
exercises.explanation: Polite way to ask someone's last name: 您贵姓? Reply with 我姓 + your surname.

exercises.prompt: Build: "Nice to meet you" (literally: meeting you very happy)
exercises.answer: 认识 你 很 高兴

exercises.prompt: You meet someone new. They say 你好, 我叫王明. What do you say back?
options: 你好, 我叫... 认识你很高兴
exercises.answer: 你好, 我叫... 认识你很高兴
exercises.explanation: Mirror the greeting and add "nice to meet you" — that's the standard A1 introduction.

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Count, ask how many, give your age

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一万 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 万 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 两
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 两 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.
Asking how many
几 (jǐ) asks "how many?" for small expected counts (under ~10). 多少 (duō shǎo) asks "how much/many?" for any quantity, including money and big numbers.

rows.translation: How old are you? (to a child)

lessons.title: One to five
lessons.description: Count from 一 to 五

exercises.explanation: 四 sounds similar to 死 (sǐ, "death") — for this reason 4 is sometimes considered unlucky in Chinese culture, like 13 in the West.
三 (sān) — first tone, high and flat. Don't confuse with 四 (sì), fourth tone, sharp falling.
四 (sì) is fourth tone — sharp falling. Compare to 三 (sān), high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which two numbers sound similar but differ only in tone?
exercises.explanation: Both have the same final "-ān/-ì" feel — distinguish by tone: 三 high-flat, 四 sharp-falling.

exercises.prompt: Order the numbers from one to five
exercises.answer: 一 二 三 四 五

exercises.explanation: Just one stroke — the simplest character in Chinese.
二 (èr) — fourth tone, sharp falling. Quick to say.
八 (bā) sounds like 发 (fā, "to prosper") — making 8 the luckiest number in Chinese culture.
九 (jiǔ) is third tone — dipping. Long and dramatic compared to other tones.
十 (shí) is second tone — rising. Don't confuse with 四 (sì), fourth tone.

exercises.prompt: Order the numbers from six to ten
exercises.answer: 六 七 八 九 十

exercises.prompt: Which number is considered the luckiest in Chinese culture?
exercises.explanation: 八 (bā) rhymes with 发 (fā, "to prosper"). Phone numbers and license plates with many 8s sell at a premium.

exercises.prompt: Order the digits in ascending order: 8, 6, 9, 7
exercises.answer: 六 七 八 九

exercises.explanation: 十五 = 10 + 5. Order matters!
Read left to right: 七 (7) × 十 (10) + 二 (2) = 72.

exercises.prompt: "九十九" (jiǔ shí jiǔ) is the number ___

exercises.explanation: 四十 = 40, then add 五 = 45. The pattern: tens-digit + 十 + units-digit.
百 (bǎi) is the unit for hundreds — 一百 = 100, 二百 = 200.
Listen for the order: 二十一 = 21 ("two-ten-one"), 十二 = 12 ("ten-two").
十二 = 10 + 2. Compare: 二十 = 2 × 10 = 20. The order of 十 and the digit reverses the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Use 几 or 多少? "How many people are in your family?"
options: 多少 — could be a big number
exercises.explanation: 几 (jǐ) for under ~10, things you can count on fingers. 多少 (duō shǎo) for any quantity, including money and large numbers.

exercises.prompt: Build: "How old are you?" (to a child)
exercises.explanation: 几岁 is for kids; for adults use 你多大?

exercises.prompt: "我二十岁" means "I am ___ years old"
exercises.explanation: No 是 needed — 我二十岁, not 我是二十岁. Age uses adjective-like structure.

exercises.prompt: Which question would you ask an adult their age?
exercises.explanation: 几岁 is for children. 多大 (literally "how big") is the polite ask for adults.
多少钱 (duō shǎo qián) — "how much money?" The phrase you'll use most when shopping.

exercises.answer: 我 有 三 个 哥哥
exercises.explanation: Numbers always need a measure word before a noun: 三个哥哥, not 三哥哥.

lessons.title: Phone numbers & dates
lessons.description: Read digits one at a time

exercises.prompt: When reading a phone number aloud, how is each digit spoken?
options: One digit at a time, like "yī sān bā"
Grouped as full numbers, like "yī bǎi sān shí bā"
Skipped — only key ones are said
exercises.answer: One digit at a time, like "yī sān bā"
exercises.explanation: Phone numbers, addresses, and ID numbers are read digit-by-digit — same as in English.

exercises.prompt: When dictating a phone number, the digit "1" is often pronounced as ___ instead of "yī"
exercises.explanation: 幺 (yāo) replaces 一 (yī) in spoken digit strings to avoid confusing 一 with 七 (qī). You'll hear it on the phone and at the bank.
零 is the formal zero. You'll also see 〇 (a circle) used in dates and ID numbers.
Years are read digit-by-digit + 年 (nián, year). 二零二四年 = "two-zero-two-four year."
月 by itself means moon/month. With a number: 一月 = January, 二月 = February.
Months are number + 月. 三月 = March (3rd month). Don't confuse 月 (month) with 日 (day).

exercises.prompt: Build the date: "May 6th" (5月 then day-number then 号)
exercises.answer: 五 月 六 号
exercises.explanation: 号 (hào) is the casual word for date/day. 日 (rì) is the formal equivalent — both follow the day number.
Big to small: 六月 (June) comes before 十号 (10th). Don't reverse it like English "the 10th of June."

exercises.prompt: Chinese dates go in what order?
exercises.explanation: Chinese always reads dates from largest unit to smallest: 2024年5月6日. Same logic for time: hour first, minute last.
Literally: "Today which month, which date?" The everyday way to ask the date.

topics.title: Basics
topics.description: Yes, no, I, you, this, that

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.
Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.
Negation: 不 vs 没
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 没 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

rows.source: 我 不 喝 茶。
我 没 有 钱。

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

rows.source: 昨天 我 吃 米饭。
明天 我 吃 米饭。

exercises.explanation: "不是" literally "is not" — a common way to say "no".

exercises.prompt: Mandarin has no single word for "yes/no." Instead, you reply with the ___
options: Verb itself, optionally negated with 不
exercises.answer: Verb itself, optionally negated with 不
exercises.explanation: Q: 你喝茶吗? (Do you drink tea?) → A: 喝 (yes, drink) or 不喝 (no, don't drink). Mirror the verb.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right negation: ___ 喝 茶。(I don't drink tea.)
exercises.explanation: 不 (bù) negates present/future and adjectives. 没 (méi) is for past actions and 有.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right negation: 我 ___ 有 钱。(I don't have money.)
exercises.explanation: 有 (have) is the one verb that's always negated with 没, never 不. 没有 is fixed.

exercises.answer: 我 不 是 学生

exercises.explanation: 不 before a fourth tone (是, shì) shifts to second tone — pronounced "bú shì."
对 is the closest word to a casual "yes" — confirms what someone said. Reverse: 不对 ("no, that's wrong").

exercises.prompt: Build a negative reply to 你是中国人吗? — "I am not Chinese"
exercises.answer: 我 不 是 中国 人
exercises.explanation: Mirror the verb 是 in the question and negate with 不: 不是. Don't add a separate "no" word.
我没有 = "I don't have." 没 always pairs with 有, never 不.
Add "们" to make a plural pronoun: 我们 = we.
你 + 们 = you (plural). English doesn't always distinguish singular/plural "you," but Mandarin does.
Adjectives don't take 是 — 我们很好, not 我们是好.
您 is the formal "you" for elders, customers, strangers. The character has a 心 (heart) under 你 — "you with my heart."

exercises.prompt: The polite form of 你 is ___
exercises.explanation: 您 is used in shops, on the phone, with elders. Don't use it with close friends — feels stiff.
我们 (wǒ men) — listen for the third tone on 我.

options: 我们 是 中国人
我 不 是 中国人

exercises.answer: 你们 是 我 的 朋友
exercises.explanation: 的 (de) makes a possessive: 我的 = "my," 你的 = "your."
您 (nín) — second tone, similar to 你 (nǐ, third tone). Listen for the rising vs dipping pitch.

exercises.prompt: 他 (he) and 她 (she) — what's the difference?
options: Different meanings (one is for adults, one for kids)
exercises.explanation: In speech, you can't tell — context decides. The 女 radical in 她 marks female; 它 (also tā) is for animals/things.
他们 is used for groups that are mixed-gender or all-male. 她们 is used only for all-female groups.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun is used for animals or inanimate objects?
exercises.explanation: 它 (tā) — same pronunciation as 他/她 but written with the radical 宀 (roof). Use it for pets, things, weather.
他们 (tā men) — first tone on 他, neutral on 们. In speech, identical to 她们.

exercises.answer: 她 是 我 姐姐

exercises.prompt: A group of three women — which is correct?
exercises.explanation: All-female groups use 她们. Add a single male and most speakers switch to 他们.

exercises.prompt: "她" is written with the radical ___ to mark female
exercises.explanation: 女 (nǚ) means "woman" — placed on the left side of 她 to distinguish it from 他.
它 (tā) — same sound as 他 and 她, but a different character. Use for pets, weather, things.

exercises.answer: 这 是 我 妈妈

exercises.explanation: 个 (ge) is the all-purpose measure word. 这个 = "this (item)," 那个 = "that (item)."
这 (zhè) — fourth tone, sharp falling. 那 (nà) is also fourth tone but starts with "n."

exercises.prompt: You're at a market and want to ask the price of a specific item. Pointing at it, you say:
exercises.explanation: 这个 + 多少钱 = "this one, how much money?" The pointing-and-asking phrase you'll use most often shopping.

exercises.answer: 那 不 是 我 的 书

exercises.explanation: 些 (xiē) marks plural "these/those." 这些 = these, 那些 = those.
这 (zhè) and 那 (nà) — both fourth tone. Distinguish by the 'zh' vs 'n' onset.
妈 (mā, first tone, high-flat) means "mom." Compare to 马 (mǎ, third tone) — "horse"!

exercises.prompt: 妈 (mā) means "mom." What does 马 (mǎ) mean?
exercises.explanation: Same syllable, different tone. 妈 (first tone) = mom; 马 (third tone) = horse. Tones matter!

exercises.answer: 我 妈妈 和 我 爸爸
exercises.explanation: 和 (hé) means "and" — used between nouns, not between full sentences.
父 = father, 母 = mother. The compact, slightly formal way to say "parents."
家 covers both "home" and "family" — context decides.

exercises.answer: 我 妈妈 在 家
exercises.explanation: 在 (zài) marks location — "at." The structure is: subject + 在 + place.

exercises.prompt: Why does Mandarin distinguish 哥哥 vs 弟弟 instead of using one word for "brother"?
options: Birth order matters in Chinese family relationships
It doesn't — they mean the same thing
exercises.answer: Birth order matters in Chinese family relationships
exercises.explanation: Chinese family terms encode age. You can't say "brother" without specifying older or younger — culture baked into vocabulary.
弟弟 (dì di) — fourth tone followed by neutral. Compare to 妹妹 (mèi mei), also fourth + neutral, but starts with "m."

exercises.answer: 我 有 一 个 姐姐
exercises.explanation: Numbers need a measure word: 一个姐姐, not 一姐姐.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My older brother is at school"
exercises.answer: 我 哥哥 在 学校

exercises.explanation: 兄 = older brother, 弟 = younger brother. Together: brothers as a category — also used between male friends.

exercises.prompt: 爷爷 and 奶奶 are which side of the family?
exercises.explanation: 爷爷 (paternal grandpa) and 奶奶 (paternal grandma). Mother's side has different terms — 外公 and 外婆.
外 (wài) literally "outside" — marks mother's-side relatives because traditionally a wife joined her husband's family.
爷爷 (yé ye) — second tone followed by neutral. The 'y' sound starts both syllables.
外 (mom's side) + 公 (granddad).

exercises.answer: 我 奶奶 八十 岁
exercises.explanation: Age skips 是: 我奶奶八十岁, not 我奶奶是八十岁.

exercises.prompt: Which is the most respectful way to address an elderly stranger?
exercises.explanation: 您 (nín) shows respect for elders. 你 with strangers older than you can feel rude.
长 (zhǎng) = senior, 辈 (bèi) = generation. Refers to older relatives collectively.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My maternal grandpa is at home"
exercises.answer: 我 外公 在 家
这 是 我 爸爸

exercises.prompt: Tap the family member you hear

exercises.answer: 我 家 有 五 个 人
exercises.explanation: 我家有X个人 is the standard pattern for "my family has X people." Note: no "de" needed.

exercises.prompt: Q: 你家有几个人? (How many people are in your family?) Why 几 and not 多少?
options: Family is a small expected count — 几 fits
多少 only works with money
There is no rule — both are equally common
exercises.answer: Family is a small expected count — 几 fits
exercises.explanation: 几 for under ~10 (people, items). 多少 for big or unknown numbers (money, populations).
全 (quán) = entire/whole. Used when emphasizing "everyone in the family."

exercises.prompt: Build: "My older sister has a daughter"
exercises.answer: 我 姐姐 有 一 个 女儿

exercises.prompt: Someone shows you a photo of their family. They point and say 这是我妈妈. The natural response is:
exercises.explanation: 漂亮 (piào liang) means "beautiful." A common compliment when shown family photos.
Listen for 四 (sì, fourth tone) — sharp falling — vs 十 (shí, second tone) rising.
Mandarin uncle terms split by age and side. 叔叔 specifically = dad's younger brother.
阿姨 is also used as a friendly term for any middle-aged woman — like English "ma'am."
表 (biǎo) marks cousins from outside the direct family line — usually mom's-side cousins.
猫 (māo) — first tone, sounds like "meow," easy to remember.
宠 = to spoil/dote, 物 = thing. Together: "a thing you spoil" — a pet.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I have one dog and one cat"
exercises.answer: 我 有 一 只 狗 和 一 只 猫
exercises.explanation: 只 (zhī) is the measure word for animals: 一只狗, 一只猫. (Not 个!)

exercises.prompt: What's the measure word for most animals (dogs, cats, birds)?
exercises.explanation: 只 (zhī) covers most small animals. Fish and snakes use 条 (long things). Don't use 个 for animals.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My cousin (older male) is in Beijing"
exercises.answer: 我 表哥 在 北京

topics.title: Food & drink
topics.description: Order, eat, and drink in Chinese

exercises.explanation: 茶 (chá, second tone) means tea. Don't confuse with 差 (chà, fourth tone) — "bad / lacking."
面 (miàn) = noodles. Often combined: 面条 (noodle strips), 拉面 (pulled noodles).
喝 is for liquids. For solids, use 吃 (chī, eat). 喝水, 喝茶, 喝咖啡.

exercises.prompt: Use 喝 (drink) or 吃 (eat)? "___ 米饭"
exercises.explanation: Rice is solid → 吃饭. Soup is borderline — 喝汤 (drink soup) is the convention.

exercises.prompt: What does "杯" (bēi) do in "一杯茶"?
options: It's the measure word for cup-shaped servings
exercises.answer: It's the measure word for cup-shaped servings
exercises.explanation: Mandarin requires a measure word between number and noun. 杯 (cup) is used for any liquid in a cup.
牛 = cow, 奶 = milk. Literally "cow milk".
咖啡 (kā fēi) — both syllables first tone, high and flat. A loanword from English "coffee."

exercises.prompt: Build: "I want a cup of coffee"
exercises.answer: 我 要 一 杯 咖啡

exercises.prompt: You're at a café. The barista asks 你要什么? You want a coffee. Best response:
exercises.explanation: 我要 + measure word + drink = the standard ordering pattern.

exercises.prompt: "请" (qǐng) at the start of a request means ___
exercises.explanation: 请给我一杯水 = "Please give me a cup of water." Adding 请 makes any request polite.
西 = west, 瓜 = melon. "Western melon" — historically came along the Silk Road from the west.
水 = water, 果 = fruit. Literally "water-fruit" — emphasizes juicy/fresh produce.
橘子 typically refers to mandarin oranges. 橙子 (chéng zi) is the larger, sweet orange.

exercises.answer: 我 喜欢 吃 苹果

exercises.explanation: 草 = grass, 莓 = berry. Strawberries grow close to the ground — "grass-berry."

exercises.prompt: Which fruit name uses the same character as the place name 葡萄牙 (Portugal)?
exercises.explanation: 葡萄 (grape) — the wine country was named for the fruit. Useful mnemonic!

exercises.prompt: Build: "I want one apple and two bananas"
exercises.answer: 我 要 一 个 苹果 和 两 个 香蕉
exercises.explanation: Use 两 (liǎng), not 二, before measure words. 两个香蕉, not 二个香蕉.

exercises.answer: 我 要 吃 米饭

exercises.explanation: 午 = noon. The midday meal.

exercises.prompt: What's the most idiomatic way to ask "have you eaten?" — a common Chinese greeting?
exercises.explanation: 你吃饭了吗? is a friendly cultural greeting — equivalent to "how are you?" in some regions. The 了 marks completion.

exercises.answer: 我 现在 吃 早饭

exercises.explanation: 点心 literally "touch the heart" — small bites between meals. The Cantonese pronunciation "dim sum" went global.
我饿了 = "I'm hungry now" (with completion 了). The 了 here marks the change of state.
早 (zǎo, third tone) — listen for the dipping pitch.
饺子 are crescent-shaped, traditionally eaten at Chinese New Year because their shape resembles ancient gold ingots.
包 (bāo) means "to wrap" — a fluffy bun wrapping meat or vegetable filling.
Soup is the borderline case for 喝/吃 — Mandarin uses 喝汤 ("drink soup").
鸡 (jī) sounds similar to 几 (jǐ, "how many") — distinguish by tone.
鱼 (yú, second tone) sounds like 余 (yú, "surplus") — fish are eaten at New Year for prosperity.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I want to eat dumplings and drink soup"
exercises.answer: 我 要 吃 饺子 和 喝 汤
exercises.explanation: Repeat the verb after 和 — Mandarin doesn't reuse one verb across two objects when they take different verbs.

exercises.prompt: You're at a restaurant. The waiter says 你要点什么? You want chicken with rice. Best response:

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.
Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜欢
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

exercises.prompt: 去 (qù) and 来 (lái) — what's the key difference?
options: 去 means moving away from speaker; 来 means moving toward speaker
去 is past tense; 来 is future tense
去 is for people; 来 is for things
exercises.answer: 去 means moving away from speaker; 来 means moving toward speaker
exercises.explanation: Same as English go/come — perspective from the speaker.
去 (qù) — fourth tone, sharp falling. Compare to 来 (lái), second tone rising.

exercises.answer: 他 来 我 家

exercises.explanation: 我去, 你去, 他去, 我们去 — same verb every time. Time and number come from other words.
去吃饭 = "go eat" — verb chains in Mandarin string actions in sequence.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right verb: ordering at a café — "I'll have a coffee."
options: 我要 一 杯 咖啡
我想 一 杯 咖啡
我喜欢 一 杯 咖啡
我有 一 杯 咖啡
exercises.answer: 我要 一 杯 咖啡
exercises.explanation: 要 (yào) is decisive — "I want / I'll have." Use it when ordering. 想 (xiǎng) is softer ("would like").

exercises.prompt: Pick the right verb: "I'd like to drink tea." (softer wish)
exercises.explanation: 想 + verb = "would like to (verb)." Notice: 想 needs another verb after it. 要 can stand alone with a noun.
爱 is stronger than 喜欢. Reserved for family, partners, deep affection — though usage is loosening among young Chinese.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I would like to go to school"
exercises.answer: 我 想 去 学校

exercises.prompt: What's wrong with: "我喜欢一杯咖啡"?
options: 喜欢 means general preference, not a one-time order
杯 is not a measure word
exercises.answer: 喜欢 means general preference, not a one-time order
exercises.explanation: 喜欢 = "I like coffee in general." To order one cup, use 要: 我要一杯咖啡.
想 (xiǎng, third tone) — listen for the dipping pitch. Don't confuse with 要 (yào, fourth tone falling).

exercises.prompt: When ordering at a restaurant, the most natural verb is ___
exercises.explanation: 要 (yào) signals decisive intent — perfect for ordering. 想 sounds more like "considering it."
看 covers seeing, looking, watching, AND reading — context decides. 看书 = read a book; 看电影 = watch a movie.

exercises.prompt: What does "听音乐" (tīng yīn yuè) mean?

exercises.explanation: 听 (tīng) — first tone, high and flat. Don't confuse with 停 (tíng, "stop").

exercises.answer: 我 在 看 书
exercises.explanation: 在 + verb = ongoing action ("am doing"). It marks the present continuous.
电 = electric, 影 = shadow. Together: "electric shadows" — a movie.

exercises.prompt: Which verb pair are you most likely to confuse?
exercises.explanation: Both have similar consonants and vowels — distinguish by tone (听 first, 停 second) and the radical (听 has 口, mouth).

exercises.answer: 他 在 听 音乐
我 有 一 个 妹妹
exercises.explanation: "个" is the most common measure word.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I don't have money"?
exercises.explanation: 有 always negates with 没, never 不. 没有 is set.

exercises.prompt: 买 (mǎi) and 卖 (mài) — what's the trick to telling them apart?
options: 买 (third tone, dipping) = buy; 卖 (fourth tone, falling) = sell
买 has fewer strokes than 卖
They're regional variants of the same word
买 is informal; 卖 is formal
exercises.answer: 买 (third tone, dipping) = buy; 卖 (fourth tone, falling) = sell
exercises.explanation: Same syllable, different tone. Mnemonic: 卖 has 十 on top — it's been "sold" so it has "more" stuff on it.
买 (mǎi, third tone — dipping) means "buy." 卖 (mài, fourth tone — sharp falling) means "sell."
Sharp falling tone — 卖 (sell). Don't confuse with 买 (buy, third tone dipping).
做 = make, 饭 = meal/rice. Together: "make a meal." The everyday word for cooking at home.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I want to buy a book"
exercises.answer: 我 要 买 一 本 书
exercises.explanation: 本 (běn) is the measure word for books and notebooks. Don't use 个 with 书.

exercises.prompt: What does "做什么" (zuò shén me) mean?
exercises.explanation: 做什么 — "do what?" Often shortened in speech to "干嘛" (gàn má) — the more colloquial version.

exercises.prompt: 买 vs 卖 — to remember which is which: 卖 has 十 on top, like ___
exercises.explanation: Mnemonic: 卖 has 十 stacked on 买 — the seller has more stuff. Helps separate the two characters.

topics.title: Places
topics.description: Here, there, home, and around town

exercises.prompt: What does "在" (zài) mean as a verb?
options: To be at / to be located
exercises.answer: To be at / to be located
exercises.explanation: 在 + place = "to be at (place)." Sentence: 我在家 = "I'm at home." No need for 是.

exercises.prompt: "哪儿" (nǎr) is the northern variant of ___
exercises.explanation: Beijing and northern speakers often replace 里 (lǐ) with 儿 (r) — adding an "er" sound. Both mean "where."
哪 (nǎ, third tone — dipping) vs 那 (nà, fourth tone — sharp falling). Tone is the only difference.

exercises.prompt: Q: 你在哪里? A best response could be:
exercises.explanation: Mirror the structure: 在 + place. 我在家 = "I'm at home."

exercises.answer: 我 爸爸 在 哪里

exercises.explanation: 客 (guest) + 厅 (hall) — "guest hall." The room where you receive guests.
Polite term — literally "hand-washing room." In restaurants, ask "洗手间在哪里?" instead of 厕所 (more direct).

exercises.prompt: Build: "My mom is in the kitchen"
exercises.answer: 我 妈妈 在 厨房

exercises.prompt: Where would you ask 洗手间在哪里?
exercises.explanation: It's the polite "where's the restroom?" — appropriate in any public place.
花 = flower, 园 = garden. Together: "flower garden."
卧 (wò) — to lie down. 卧室 = "lying-down room" = bedroom. 教室 (jiào shì) = classroom — different first character.
医 = medicine/doctor, 院 = courtyard/institution. Together: medical institution.
银 = silver, 行 = business/firm. Note: 行 is read "háng" here, not "xíng" — same character, different meanings.
学校 (xué xiào) — second tone + fourth tone. All four options share 学 (study).
公 = public, 园 = garden. "Public garden" = park.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My friend is at the restaurant"
exercises.answer: 我 朋友 在 饭馆
我 的 家 在 哪里

exercises.explanation: 很 + adjective is the standard "very (adj)" structure. 远 = far.
Position is sandwiched: 在 + place + 上 (on) / 下 (under) / 里 (inside). E.g., 在桌子上 = on the table.
近 (jìn) means "near." Same syllable as 进 (jìn, "enter") and 今 (jīn, "now/today") — distinguish by context.

exercises.answer: 我 家 很 远
exercises.explanation: Adjectives don't need 是. 很 acts as a placeholder before the adjective.
在屋子里 = "inside the room." Pairs of position words: 里/外 (in/out), 上/下 (up/down).
旁 = side, 边 = edge. 在...旁边 = "next to (something)."

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Days, hours, and when things happen

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 点 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.
Time-words come first
In Mandarin, time goes before the verb. Compare:

rows.source: 我 明天 去 学校。
rows.translation: I am going to school tomorrow.

rows.source: 他 今天 不 来。

sections.text: A handy memory trick: Chinese says time in big-to-small order — year, month, day, hour, minute. The opposite of how dates are spoken in English.

exercises.explanation: 后 = after. 后天 = "after-tomorrow" — the day after tomorrow. Compare 前天 = day before yesterday.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I will go to school tomorrow"
exercises.answer: 我 明天 去 学校
exercises.explanation: Time words go BEFORE the verb in Mandarin — never at the end like English.
前 = before. 前天 = day before yesterday. Pair: 后天 = day after tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Q: 你昨天去哪里? (Where did you go yesterday?) — How does Mandarin show "yesterday/past"?
options: With the time word 昨天 — verbs don't change
By adding 是 before the verb
By using a special past-tense particle
exercises.answer: With the time word 昨天 — verbs don't change
exercises.explanation: Mandarin verbs are fixed. Time words do all the heavy lifting — add 昨天 for past, 明天 for future.

exercises.answer: 昨天 我 吃 饺子
exercises.explanation: Time word can also start the sentence — both 昨天我吃饺子 and 我昨天吃饺子 are correct.

exercises.prompt: What does "星期一" (xīng qī yī) mean?
Which day is the "odd one out" — not built with a number?
exercises.explanation: All other days are 星期 + a digit (一 to 六). Sunday is special: 星期天 (casual) or 星期日 (formal).
周 = week, 末 = end. The weekend (Saturday + Sunday).
六 (liù) is fourth tone — falling. Listen for the final number.

exercises.answer: 今天 是 星期二
exercises.explanation: Days of the week DO take 是 (unlike adjectives). Today is Tuesday → 今天是星期二.

exercises.prompt: Q: 今天星期几? What does this ask?
exercises.explanation: 几 + counter is "which (one)?" — 星期几 = which day of the week. The standard way to ask the day.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I am at school on Monday"
exercises.answer: 我 星期一 在 学校

exercises.prompt: What time is "七点半" (qī diǎn bàn)?
exercises.explanation: 七点 = 7 o'clock, 半 = half. Together: half past seven (7:30).
一刻 = one quarter (15 min). Or you could say 五点十五分 — both work.
钟 (zhōng, "clock") is optional — adding it emphasizes the exact hour.
Three thirty. Listen for 半 (bàn, fourth tone) at the end.

exercises.answer: 我 七 点 起 床
exercises.explanation: 起床 (qǐ chuáng) = get out of bed. Time goes after subject, before verb.

exercises.prompt: Q: 现在几点? What's a natural answer if it's 9:30?
exercises.explanation: 九点半 is the most idiomatic. 九点三十(分) is also acceptable but feels more clinical.

exercises.prompt: Build: "It is now half past seven"
exercises.answer: 现在 七 点 半
我 现在 在 吃 饭

exercises.explanation: 前 = before/front. Pair with 后 (after/back). 以前 = formerly; 以后 = afterwards.

exercises.prompt: "马上" (mǎ shàng) literally "on a horse" — means ___
exercises.explanation: Idiom: in old China, "on horseback" meant hurried — like English "on the double."
现在 (xiàn zài) — both fourth tone, sharp falling.

exercises.answer: 我 以后 吃 饭

exercises.prompt: Your friend asks 你什么时候来? You'll be there in two minutes. Best response:
exercises.explanation: 马上来 = "coming right away." The standard response when you'll arrive imminently.
等 = wait, 一下 = a brief moment. Common in conversation when someone needs a second.
早 (zǎo) = early. 早上 = morning (roughly 6am to 9am).
晚 = late. 晚上 = evening/night (roughly 6pm onward).
中 = middle, 午 = noon. "Middle of the day."
早上好 = "good morning." Substitute 早上 with another part-of-day to greet at any hour.

exercises.prompt: How do you greet someone in the evening?
exercises.explanation: 晚上好 = "good evening." 晚安 (wǎn ān) = "good night" (used at bedtime, not as a greeting).
Said only at bedtime. NOT a greeting — that's 晚上好.

exercises.prompt: Build: "In the morning I drink coffee"
exercises.answer: 早上 我 喝 咖啡

exercises.explanation: 下 = down/after, 午 = noon. "After noon" = afternoon. Pair with 上午 = before noon (morning, formal).

guide.intro: Mandarin questions are unusually friendly to learners — there's no auxiliary "do/does", no inversion. The word order stays the same as a statement.

sections.text: The 吗 particle
For yes/no questions, take a statement and add 吗 (ma) at the end. That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

rows.source: 你 喝 茶 吗？

sections.text: Question words stay put
For information questions (who, what, where), put the question word exactly where the answer would go. No fronting like English.
Common question words
A-not-A questions
A second way to ask yes/no questions: repeat the verb with 不 between. It's a touch more direct than 吗.

rows.source: 你 是不是 学生？
rows.translation: Are you a student or not?
Do you drink tea or not?

sections.text: Don't mix patterns: 你是不是学生吗？ is wrong. Pick one of the two question forms.

exercises.prompt: In Mandarin, where does the question word go?
options: At the end, after the verb
exercises.explanation: 你是谁? = literally "You are who?" The question word stays in place — no fronting like English.
Question word 谁 goes where the answer (a name) would go — at the end after 是.

exercises.prompt: What does "为什么" literally translate to?
exercises.explanation: 为 = for/because, 什么 = what. "For what reason" = why.

exercises.prompt: "什么意思" (shén me yì si) means ___
exercises.explanation: 意思 = meaning. The handy phrase to ask the meaning of a word: ___ 什么意思?

exercises.prompt: Where does "什么时候" go in: "When are you coming?"
options: 你什么时候来 (before the verb)
什么时候你来 (at the start)
你来什么时候 (at the end)
exercises.answer: 你什么时候来 (before the verb)
exercises.explanation: Time questions follow the same rule as time words — they go AFTER the subject and BEFORE the verb.

exercises.prompt: "哪儿" (nǎr) and "哪里" (nǎ lǐ) — both mean ___
exercises.explanation: 哪儿 is northern (Beijing), 哪里 is southern. They're interchangeable — pick one and stick with it.
去 (qù) means "go." 你去哪里 = "Where are you going?"

exercises.prompt: Build: "When do you go to school?"
exercises.answer: 你 什么 时候 去 学校

exercises.explanation: Literally: "You are where person?" The standard way to ask someone's hometown/origin.
Q: 你是哪国人? — "What nationality are you?" Reply with country + 人.

exercises.prompt: When asking the price of something, you would use ___
exercises.explanation: 钱 (qián) = money. 多少 fits any quantity — perfect for prices, which can be small or large.

exercises.prompt: Build: "How many people are in your family?"
exercises.answer: 你 家 有 几 个 人
exercises.explanation: Family is a small expected count → 几个人. Don't forget the measure word 个.

exercises.prompt: "几岁" (jǐ suì) is for asking ___'s age
exercises.explanation: 几岁 expects a small number — only fits children. For adults, use 多大 (how big) — "how old."

exercises.prompt: What does "怎么样" do in conversation?
options: Asks "how about it?" or "what do you think?"
exercises.answer: Asks "how about it?" or "what do you think?"
exercises.explanation: Versatile phrase — used to ask opinion, suggest plans, or check up on someone. "今天怎么样?" = "How was today?"

exercises.answer: 这 个 多少 钱
exercises.explanation: 这个 = "this one." The classic shopping question.

exercises.prompt: What word turns a statement into a yes/no question?
exercises.explanation: Adding 吗 at the end is like a verbal question mark.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask "Are you good?"

exercises.answer: 你 要 茶 吗

exercises.prompt: How do you turn 你喝茶 (you drink tea) into a yes/no question?
exercises.explanation: 你喝茶 → 你喝茶吗? That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

exercises.prompt: Statement: 你是中国人. Add ___ to make it a yes/no question.
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 吗 turns any statement into a yes/no question.

exercises.prompt: What's the "A-not-A" form of "do you drink tea?"
exercises.explanation: Repeat the verb with 不 between it: 喝不喝. A direct, slightly more casual alternative to 吗.

exercises.prompt: Why is 你是不是学生吗? wrong?
options: You can't combine A-not-A with 吗 — pick one
是不是 should be 不是不
exercises.answer: You can't combine A-not-A with 吗 — pick one
exercises.explanation: A-not-A and 吗 are two ways to form yes/no questions. Don't mix them.

exercises.answer: 你 是 不 是 学生

exercises.prompt: Statement: 他是学生. The yes/no question (with 吗) is: 他是学生 ___
exercises.explanation: Add 吗 at the end. Yes/no questions don't change word order.

topics.title: Directions
topics.description: Left, right, north, south, ask the way

lessons.title: Left, right, straight
lessons.description: The three directions you need most

exercises.explanation: 面 (miàn) = side/face. Add it to direction words: 前面 (in front), 后面 (behind), 左面 (left side).
左 (zuǒ, third tone — dipping) means "left." Don't confuse with 走 (zǒu, also third tone) — "walk."
向 (xiàng) = toward. 拐 (guǎi) = turn. "Turn (toward) left".

exercises.prompt: What does "向右拐" (xiàng yòu guǎi) mean?

exercises.answer: 直走 然后 向 左 拐
exercises.explanation: 然后 (rán hòu) means "then" — connects two instructions in sequence.

exercises.prompt: What does "北京" (Běi jīng) literally mean?
exercises.explanation: 北 = north, 京 = capital. The name reflects the city's history. Compare 南京 (Nanjing) = "southern capital."
东 (dōng) — first tone, high and flat. Different from 冬 (dōng, "winter") — same sound, different character.
Compounds combine the two: 东南 = east + south = southeast. Standard intercardinal pattern.

exercises.prompt: Build: "My home is in the north"
exercises.answer: 我 家 在 北 边
exercises.explanation: 边 (biān) means "side." 北边 = the north side. Pair with 南边, 东边, 西边.

exercises.prompt: In Chinese culture, which order are cardinal directions traditionally listed?
options: East, south, west, north (东南西北)
North, south, east, west (北南东西)
North, east, south, west (北东南西)
exercises.answer: East, south, west, north (东南西北)
exercises.explanation: 东南西北 — clockwise starting from east. The Chinese mnemonic order, different from English's "north-south-east-west."

exercises.prompt: Build: "My friend lives in the south"
exercises.answer: 我 朋友 住 在 南 边
exercises.explanation: 住 (zhù) = live/reside. 住在 + place = "live in (place)."

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.description: Get pointed in the right direction

exercises.prompt: Build "How do I get to the school?"
How would you politely ask a stranger "Excuse me, where is the bank?"
exercises.explanation: 请问 (qǐng wèn) literally "please ask" — the polite "excuse me" before asking a question.
Always say 请问 before asking a stranger for directions or information. Skipping it can sound rude.
怎么 = how, 走 = walk/go. "How to get there?" The standard navigation question.

exercises.prompt: Build: "How do I get to the hospital?"
Q: 银行在哪里? Possible answer: "在前面的路口左拐." What does this mean?
options: Turn left at the intersection ahead
exercises.answer: Turn left at the intersection ahead
exercises.explanation: 前面 = ahead, 路口 = intersection, 左拐 = turn left. A common direction-giving phrase.
过 (guò) = pass through. 马路 = main road. Useful when giving directions in cities.

exercises.prompt: What does "自行车" (zì xíng chē) mean?
exercises.explanation: 自行车 literally "self-go-vehicle" — a vehicle that goes by itself (i.e., no engine, just legs).
出租 = rent out, 车 = vehicle. A "rental car" — by the trip.
走 = walk, 路 = road. "Walk the road" — go on foot.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I take the subway to school"
exercises.answer: 我 坐 地铁 去 学校
exercises.explanation: 坐 (zuò) = sit/take (transport). 坐 + vehicle + 去 + place = take (vehicle) to (place).

exercises.prompt: What does "骑" (qí) refer to as a verb?
exercises.explanation: 骑自行车 (ride a bike), 骑马 (ride a horse). For cars, use 开 (drive). For taxis/buses, use 坐 (sit/take).
开 = open/start. "Start the vehicle" — drive.

exercises.prompt: Which color is associated with luck and celebration in Chinese culture?
exercises.explanation: Red signals luck, joy, and prosperity. New Year decorations, wedding dresses, and 红包 (red envelopes for cash gifts) are all red.
红 (hóng, second tone — rising). Used in many compound words: 红色 (red color), 红茶 (black tea, literally "red tea").

exercises.prompt: Color names usually combine with ___ to mean "X color"
exercises.explanation: 色 (sè) = color. 红色 = red color. You can sometimes drop 色 in fixed phrases.

exercises.answer: 我 的 书 是 红 色

exercises.explanation: Color word + 色. Note: 黄色 in some contexts (films, websites) also implies "adult content" — like English "blue" used for similar reasons.
蓝 (lán) — blue. 篮 (lán) — basket (as in 篮球, basketball). Same sound, different characters.

exercises.prompt: In Chinese culture, white is traditionally associated with ___
exercises.explanation: White is the funeral color in Chinese tradition. Don't gift white flowers or wear all white to a Chinese wedding.
白 (bái) — white. Same syllable as 百 (bǎi, hundred), 拜 (bài, worship). Tones distinguish them.
绿 = green, 茶 = tea. The unfermented variety, popular for daily drinking.

exercises.prompt: What does "红茶" (hóng chá) literally translate to?
options: Red tea (= black tea in English)
exercises.answer: Red tea (= black tea in English)
exercises.explanation: Chinese names tea by the brewed color (red), English by the leaf color (black). Same drink, different perspective.

exercises.answer: 我 喜欢 白 色 的 猫
exercises.explanation: 白色的猫 — "of-white-color cat." 的 (de) attaches the color phrase to the noun.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask "What color is it?"

exercises.answer: 苹果 是 红 色
exercises.explanation: 色 (sè) means "color" — pair with the color character.

exercises.prompt: How would you ask "What color is your car?"
exercises.explanation: Pattern: subject + 是 + 什么颜色?

exercises.answer: 这 只 狗 是 黑 色
exercises.explanation: 只 is the measure word for animals.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I like the color red"?

exercises.explanation: 粉 = powder. "Powder color" — like rouge or makeup. The everyday word for pink.
橙 (chéng) — also means the orange fruit. Same word in Mandarin for the fruit and the color.

exercises.answer: 我 喜欢 粉 色 的 花

exercises.explanation: 棕 = palm tree (the brown trunk). Used for chocolate, soil, brown hair.
灰 (huī) literally "ash." Used metaphorically too: 灰心 ("ash heart") = discouraged.
紫 (zǐ) — purple. Third tone, dipping.

exercises.answer: 我 奶奶 的 头发 是 灰 色
exercises.explanation: 头发 (tóu fa) = hair. 我奶奶的头发 = "my grandma's hair."
阴 = shaded, overcast. The opposite of 晴 (sunny). Weather forecasts use 多云 (mostly cloudy) and 阴 (overcast).
下 (xià) = come down/fall. 下雨 literally "rain falling." 下雪 = snowing.

exercises.answer: 今天 天气 很 好
exercises.explanation: Weather adjectives don't take 是. Use 很 + adjective.
刮 = blow/scrape. 刮风 = the wind blows.
天 = sky/day, 气 = air. Together: "sky-air" = weather.
Pleasantly warm — between cool and hot. The mid-range, comfortable temperature.
Pleasantly cool — like a breeze on a hot day. Different from 冷 (cold/uncomfortable).
热 (rè) — fourth tone, sharp falling. Single syllable for "hot."
今天热 alone is fine but 今天很热 sounds more natural — 很 cushions the adjective.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "It's not cold today"?
exercises.explanation: Negate adjectives with 不, NOT 没. 不冷 (not cold), 不热 (not hot).
秋 = harvest season. 天 = day/sky. Pattern across all seasons: season-character + 天.
冬 (dōng, first tone) — winter. Same sound as 东 (east) — distinguish by character.

exercises.prompt: Q: 你喜欢什么季节? Best answer: "___ 喜欢春天"
exercises.explanation: Mirror the question — substitute 你 with 我 and answer.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I like summer because it's hot"
exercises.answer: 我 喜欢 夏天 因为 很 热
exercises.explanation: 因为 (yīn wèi) means "because" — the standard reason connector.
Standalone word for "season" — distinct from 春天/夏天 etc., which mean specific seasons.

exercises.prompt: In which season does it usually 下雪 (snow) in Beijing?
All four seasons end with the same character ___
exercises.explanation: 春天, 夏天, 秋天, 冬天 — each is season-character + 天 (day/sky). Easy pattern to remember.
打 = strike/hit, 雷 = thunder. "Thunder strikes."
Useful when 下雨! 雨伞 (yǔ sǎn) = rain umbrella.
雪 (xuě) — snow. Third tone with the harder 'x' onset, like a hiss.

exercises.answer: 明天 天气 很 晴

exercises.prompt: Q: 明天天气怎么样? Best answer for "It might rain":
exercises.explanation: 可能 (kě néng) = maybe / possibly. Common in weather forecasts.

exercises.answer: 你 好 我 叫 小明

exercises.explanation: 苹果 (píng guǒ) — apple.
Same syllable, different tone. 买 (third tone) buy, 卖 (fourth tone) sell.

exercises.prompt: Build: "I want a cup of coffee"
exercises.answer: 我 要 一 杯 咖啡

options: Adjectives don't take 是 — say 我很好
exercises.answer: Adjectives don't take 是 — say 我很好
我 妈妈 在 哪里

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct: "I have one dog"?
exercises.explanation: 只 (zhī) is the measure word for animals. Don't use 个 with animals.

exercises.prompt: Build: "Tomorrow I will go to school"
exercises.answer: 明天 我 去 学校

exercises.prompt: What's the right negation for 我 ___ 有 钱?
exercises.explanation: 有 always negates with 没, never 不.

exercises.prompt: Build "I want to drink a cup of tea"
exercises.answer: 我 要 喝 一 杯 茶

exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask a stranger "where is the bathroom?"
options: 请问, 洗手间在哪里?
exercises.answer: 请问, 洗手间在哪里?
exercises.explanation: 请问 = polite "excuse me." 洗手间 (washroom) is gentler than 厕所 (toilet) for strangers.

exercises.prompt: 妈 (mā) is to "mom" as 马 (mǎ) is to ___
exercises.explanation: Same syllable, different tone — completely different meaning. Tones matter!

exercises.answer: 你 叫 什么 名字

exercises.prompt: Mandarin time-words go ___ in a sentence
options: At the end of the sentence
exercises.explanation: Time goes BEFORE the verb (or at the very start). 我明天去 — never 我去明天.
